subhead: Take a free practice quiz or get instant, explained answers to OSHA 10-hour training questions — hazard recognition, PPE, and workers' rights, without the guesswork.
metaTitle: OSHA 10-Hour Training Quiz & Practice Questions | Cambo
metaDescription: Free OSHA 10-hour Outreach quiz and practice questions with instant, explained answers. Hazard recognition, fall protection, PPE, and workers' rights.
whyItWorks: OSHA 10-hour material covers a lot of distinct hazard categories — fall protection, electrical, PPE, hazard communication — and it's easy to mix up which standard applies to which scenario. Cambo reads the exact question and explains the specific rule behind the answer.

sampleQuestions.q: What is the leading cause of death in the construction industry, according to OSHA?
sampleQuestions.a: Falls — they account for more construction fatalities than any other cause, which is why fall protection is one of OSHA's most emphasized topics.

sampleQuestions.q: Under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, what document provides detailed information about a chemical's hazards?
sampleQuestions.a: A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) — it details the chemical's properties, health effects, safe handling, and emergency measures.

sampleQuestions.q: What color is typically used on OSHA-style signage to indicate a hazard that could result in death or serious injury?
sampleQuestions.a: Red — ANSI-based signage convention uses red for "Danger" (immediate serious hazard), orange for "Warning," and yellow for "Caution."

sampleQuestions.q: Under OSHA's fall protection standard, at what height is fall protection generally required in general industry?
sampleQuestions.a: 4 feet — general industry requires fall protection at 4 feet, though the threshold is different for construction (6 feet) and some other specific industries.

sampleQuestions.q: What does "PPE" stand for, and who is generally responsible for providing it?
options: Personal Protective Equipment — employees must purchase their own
Personal Protective Equipment — employers are generally required to provide it at no cost to employees
Preventive Protection Enforcement — provided by the OSHA regional office
Personal Protective Equipment — provided by the general contractor only on construction sites
sampleQuestions.a: Personal Protective Equipment — employers are generally required to provide PPE at no cost to employees when it's needed to protect against workplace hazards.

sampleQuestions.q: What is a worker's right if they believe a task poses an imminent danger to their safety?
options: They must complete the task and file a complaint with OSHA afterward
They may stop work only if a supervisor agrees the hazard is real
They have the right to refuse the task and report the hazard without fear of retaliation
They may refuse only if they are a member of a union
sampleQuestions.a: The right to refuse the task and report the hazard without fear of retaliation — OSHA's General Duty Clause and whistleblower protections cover this, and it's a core topic in the required workers' rights block.

faqs.q: Is the OSHA 10-hour card a certification?
faqs.a: No — OSHA is clear that no course in the Outreach Training Program (including the 10-hour) is considered a certification. It's a completion card showing you finished the awareness-level training.

faqs.q: Is OSHA 10-hour training required by law?
faqs.a: Not by OSHA itself in most cases, though some states, cities, and individual employers require it as a condition of working on a jobsite.

faqs.q: What's the difference between the 10-hour and 30-hour courses?
faqs.a: The 10-hour is intended for entry-level workers and covers general hazard awareness. The 30-hour is more in-depth and intended for supervisors or workers with safety responsibilities.

faqs.q: How long is the OSHA 10-hour card valid?
faqs.a: OSHA doesn't set an expiration date on the card itself, though many employers and job sites require renewal every 5 years as a matter of policy.

faqs.q: What is required in every 10-hour Outreach course?
faqs.a: A minimum 2-hour block on workers' rights, employer responsibilities, and how to file a complaint — this is required across every industry version of the course.
